chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.note: The opening unit (¶1–9) is a compact cosmogonic survey in an impersonal, system-internal register (Separation of the two principles; attack of Darkness; First Man; Living Spirit’s construction; Third Ambassador; final conflagration and binding). From ¶10 onward the chapter shifts to a justificatory/protreptic frame (Mani’s books, exhortations to write, institutional categories, and comparative apostle-history), with strong editorial fatigue and institutional drift; this later material is not part of the oldest correspondential-teaching substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ad[vent] of the Apostle.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later layers: dialogue framing, apostolic/church succession doctrine, and extended NT-derived Jesus/Paraclete material. Only small fragments (¶24–25) preserve schematic cosmological “mystery” content that stays inside the Light–Darkness system (depths/heights, war, mingling, ships, Adam). Even these appear embedded in Mani’s autobiographical Paraclete-revelation rhetoric, so they are extracted as MIXED rather than CORE.

chapters.title: The Second, concerning the Parable of the Tree.
chapters.note: This chapter is front-loaded with Christian overlay: Gospel proof-texting of the two trees (¶1–3, ¶10) and NT narrative exempla (Judas/Paul; ¶7–9). The oldest teaching substrate appears mainly in the middle and second half as systematic correspondential exposition: the “good tree”/“bad tree” each having five limbs (intellectual qualities) mapped to cosmic beings/ships/realms (¶11–12, ¶15, ¶17–19, ¶22–24). Two clear editorial/institutional grafts cross the cosmos→institution boundary by identifying “taste” and salvific process with the “holy church,” teachers, catechumens, and alms (¶13, ¶16), and another applies the “bad fruits” taste to “sects” (¶20). Several paragraphs are mixed where a basically cosmological mapping has had sect/church phrases inserted (notably ¶15, ¶22, ¶24).

chapters.title: The Interpretation of Happiness, Wisdom and Power; what they signify.
chapters.note: The chapter’s core substrate is a systematic five-fold correspondential schema mapping “happiness / wisdom / power” across successive cosmic levels (Land of Light → Sun/ship of living fire → ship of living waters → elements). The opening paragraphs are a dialogue/topic-introduction frame. After the four cosmic iterations, an editor adds an institutional extension (“Now, moreover… in the holy church”), matching the prior syntactic pattern but shifting Side-B of the mapping from cosmos→church; the final line then closes with a beatitude-style exhortation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Great Days that have come forth from one another, together with the Four Nights
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by a schematic cosmological taxonomy (four Days / four Nights, each with twelve ‘hours’) in an impersonal expository voice—strongly CORE. The only clear later intrusions are brief institutional/application anchors (“his church”, “sects”, “old man”) and the formulaic opening/closing benedictions. No explicit NT citation overlay appears.

chapters.title: Concerning Four Hunters of Light and Four of Darkness.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a systematic correspondential teaching: each “hunter” is defined by a stable set of internal mappings (hunter → net/ship/sea) within Manichaean cosmic architecture. The main later intrusions are (a) dialogue frame formulas (“the apostle speaks…”) and (b) cosmos→institution/polemical pointing (“holy church”, “rules in every sect”, “erroneous teaching”), which break the substrate rule that both sides of the mapping remain inside the cosmic system. The beatitude-style closings are pastoral exhortation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Storehouses that have poured forth from the Land of Darkness since the [Beginning]; the Five Rulers, the Five Spirits, the Five Bodies, the Five Tastes.
chapters.note: Chapter is dominated by systematic pentadic cosmology (storehouses→elements→trees→genera; five kings with bodies/metals/tastes; the King of Darkness’s shapes/properties/faculties). Late editorial/application material concentrates in the second half (notably identifying dark “spirits” with contemporary institutions/practices and ending with direct exhortation to the elect), consistent with the detected fatigue drift. Several sections also show signs of redaction/corruption but remain internal to the cosmic system.

chapters.title: The Seventh, concerning the Five Fathers
chapters.note: The first half is dominated by an ordered, impersonal emanation-schema (Father → three emanations → further triads), characteristic of the systematic cosmological teaching layer. The second half shows clear editorial fatigue: institutional identifications (apostles/church), explicit elect/catechumen address (seam-flagged), and a Gospel-style citation/paraphrase (Jn 8) embedded in the third-power description.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fourteen Vehicles that Jesus has boarded.
chapters.note: ¶2–8 preserve a compact, systematic correspondential list of ten cosmic “vehicles” (ships, pillar, summons/obedience, and five living elements) used to describe Jesus’ descent through the cosmological architecture. The chapter then shows strong editorial fatigue: ¶9 is a clear institutional graft (“holy church…brothers…sisters…catechumens”), and ¶10 is a homiletic/doxological summary with a beatitude rather than further cosmological mapping.

chapters.title: The Explanation of the Peace, what it is; the Right Hand; the Kiss; the Salutation.
chapters.note: The first half preserves a coherent cosmological teaching: five ritual “signs” are primordial mysteries enacted in the descent/ascent drama of the First Man (cosmos→cosmos). From ¶10 onward the same items are repeatedly re-applied to human custom “in the midst of mankind” and then to church initiation and hierarchy (cosmos→contemporary practice), with strong second-half pastoral/application drift (editorial fatigue). A probable scriptural/Christianized enthronement formula appears inside ¶14, embedded in an otherwise cosmological sequence.

chapters.title: Concerning the Interpretation of the Fourteen [Great Aeons] of Light, about which Sethel has spoken in [his Prayer]
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a clear dialogue-frame request (disciples → apostle) and a brief promise-to-interpret. The core teaching appears as a compact, systematic fourteenfold enumeration (5+2+5+2), with cosmos→cosmos mapping (aeons/elements/sons/call-hearing/fathers) and an impersonal explanatory voice. The final paragraph preserves substantial cosmological teaching about the hidden land/plenitude and the Ambassador’s kingship, but is introduced through an interpretive link to Seth’s prayer; that Seth-prayer linkage is likely a later editorial anchoring to a gnostic tradition rather than the oldest substrate.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Interpretation of] all [the] Fathers of [Light], who are distinguished from one another.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a catechetical list built on the formula “The beginning of X is Y,” where X often names human virtues/activities (grace, prayer, builders, deliverers). That “X→Y” mapping crosses from cosmos to lived religious/social language and looks like a later didactic application-layer scaffold. Nevertheless, many lines preserve older cosmological identifications/titles of the Fathers of Light and brief functional descriptions (e.g., Living Spirit with five sons; Light Mind as awakener/gatherer). The opening attribution and the closing beatitudes are later frame/application material.

chapters.title: Concerning the Interpretation of the Five Words that are proclaimed in the Universe
chapters.note: This chapter fragment is dominated by dialogue-frame and sect-referential setup (Baptists / “Purified Ones”). The oldest recoverable layer appears only as brief enumerative identifications of the “words” with Manichaean cosmological beings (Father; Third Ambassador). The interpretive hook (“they call it by this name”) suggests the teaching is being applied to contemporary sectarian terminology, so the seam likely falls between the sectarian naming and the bare cosmological identifications.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Saviours, the Resurrectors of Those Who Are Dead, Together with the Five Resurrections
chapters.note: This kephalaion is chiefly a pentadic, systematic enumeration of five “resurrectors/saviours” with cosmological agents (Father, Light Mind, etc.). The extant text is heavily lacunose at the start (first/second items partly lost) and ends with a generalized beatitude that reads like later exhortatory/pastoral closure rather than impersonal mechanism-teaching. The opening is a clear hagiographic dialogue frame.

chapters.title: The Interpretation [of] the S[i]lence, the Fast, [the Peace], the Day, [and] the Rest; [what] they are.
chapters.note: Despite the chapter title’s ritual-sounding keywords (silence/fast/peace/day/rest), the surviving content is mostly cosmological identification/exposition (First Man, ship of living waters, Pillar of Glory, great aeon). The only clear editorial layer is the opening dialogue-question frame and a closing beatitude/doxology. Several paragraphs are heavily lacunose; where a teaching paragraph includes an explicit teacher-attribution (“the enlightener ...”), that phrase is treated as later framing and stripped, leaving the underlying cosmological explanation.

chapters.title: [Concerning the ... ...] Five [Parts ...] Worlds of [...]
chapters.note: This chapter is predominantly core cosmological teaching (pentadic structure → doubling into male/female → twelvefold complex with zodiacal linkage). It is framed by a hagiographic dialogue opening and a brief doxological close. The only clear late graft is the end application that moves from cosmic antagonists to the "holy church" and sect polemic (¶8–9), which crosses from cosmos→cosmos mapping into cosmos→institution pointing.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Five] Greatnesses who [went forth] against the Darkness.
chapters.note: Dominantly CORE: a systematic pentadic listing of the five Greatnesses (emanational series) followed by a long, internally-cosmic exposition of the five ‘advents’ via similes (judge, king inspecting works, butter in milk) and eschatological mechanics (Summons/Obedience; Last Statue; great fire). Later layers appear as (a) FRAME dialogue-attribution at the start, (b) a few small audience-address intrusions (MIXED), (c) a Christian salvation-history/tree-of-life segment tied to Adam/Eve (OVERLAY), and (d) a closing beatitude/exhortation (PASTORAL).

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Three Seasons
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological and structural: it defines the three times/seasons by anchoring them to major cosmic events (First Man’s descent/ascent; construction of the universe; Ambassador’s image → final Statue). The only later material is the dialogue/hagiographic container (“apostle…disciples” Q&A attributions), which can be cleanly stripped without damaging the underlying system-teaching. No NT citation formulae or institutional/pastoral grafts appear; “Jesus” functions as a Manichaean cosmic agent within the redemption sequence, not as Gospel overlay.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Five] War[s that the] Sons of [Li]ght waged with the Sons] of Darkness.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a core cosmological sequence: five ordered "wars" describing major salvific operations (First Living Man; Living Spirit; Third Ambassador; Jesus the glorious one; Counsel of Life). There is a thin hagiographic dialogue attribution at the opening (¶1), a clear Christian overlay via a Gospel-style citation formula (¶2), and an editorial/pastoral beatitude applying the victory-pattern to the "elect" at the end (¶9), consistent with the chapter’s second-half drift.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Releases: what they are
chapters.note: Dominantly a systematic cosmological list of five "releases" (rescues/redemptions) tied to named cosmic agents (First Man, Living Spirit, Third Ambassador, Jesus the Splendour, Great Counsel/Summons-Obedience), with heavy lacunose transmission. The main late accretion is the final eschatological-institutional paragraph about "apostles," "commandment," and judgment (¶12), plus a brief exhortative beatitude (¶13). ¶1 contains a hagiographic speech-introduction framing the core list; ¶6 contains an institutional seam (“churches”) embedded within an otherwise cosmological description of Jesus the Splendour’s saving work.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Name of the Fathers
chapters.note: After a brief dialogue frame (¶1–2), the chapter gives a compact, systematic cosmological definition of why multiple divine beings can be called “father”: each is “father” relative to his own “greatness” (a corresponding realm/vehicle in which he is established). No pastoral/application turn and no NT citation overlay; “Jesus the Splendour” functions as a cosmological entity.

chapters.title: [C]oncerning the Father of Gr[eat]ness: [ho]w he is established and determined.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly core cosmological-correspondential exposition: an impersonal, systematic description of the Father of Greatness established in five light limbs (with sensory/emanational qualities) and twelve light limbs/wisdoms, all kept entirely within the cosmic system (aeons, storehouses, limbs). Only the opening dialogue-attribution is later frame.

chapters.title: [On] the Land of Light
chapters.note: Despite heavy lacunae, the chapter is almost entirely systematic cosmological description of the Land of Light (faces/images, fivefold structures, living air, aeons, angels, gifts). There is no NT citation, no institutional material, and no Q&A frame. Only the rubric-like opening and a closing beatitude-like line read as later framing/application rather than substrate exposition.

chapters.title: [ ... ] which [ ... ]
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological narrative/substrate (origin of the assault, generation of the five dark elements, and the First Man’s arming). Only ¶1 reads as explicit redactional framing (“Once again it happened…”). ¶5 contains a clear later “teaching-about-teaching” insertion referencing “apostle[s]” (institutional/compilation voice) embedded in an otherwise core sequence.

chapters.title: Chapter 24: [... / ...]
chapters.note: Dominantly CORE cosmological exposition on measuring/contrasting temporal duration with the unmeasurable twin eternities, expressed through emanation-sequences (Great Spirit/Mother of Life/First Man/five gods; then the parallel dark process of Matter). Later editorial reflection appears where the text shifts from describing cosmic process to discussing what “apostles/teachers” can or cannot proclaim; those clauses are removed where cleanly separable.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Advent of Five Fathers from the Five Limbs of the Father]
chapters.note: A very short chapter with a clear hagiographic/dialogue frame opening, followed by a compact core correspondential teaching: a fivefold emanation/advent sequence mapping five cosmic figures to five internal faculties/limbs of the Father (mind, thought, insight, counsel, consideration). No NT citation formulae; “Jesus the Beloved” functions here as a named cosmological being within the system, not as a Gospel overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man and the Ambassador and the Ship; what they resemble.
chapters.note: A chain of five similes mapping major cosmic redeemers (First Man, Ship of the Day/Great Spirit, Living Spirit, Ambassador) onto human analogies is the dominant layer. The only clear later addition is the closing exhortation to disciples in direct second-person application voice. The opening paragraph contains a brief hagiographic dialogue-attribution that must be stripped to recover the older teaching unit.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Forms that exist in the Rulers of Darkness.
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological-correspondential description of the Ruler of Darkness (five body-forms sourced from the five dark worlds, plus additional triads of qualities). It opens with a dialogue/"apostle" frame (later compilation layer) and ends with a clear exhortatory application to the audience (pastoral/application drift), consistent with editorial fatigue in the second half.

chapters.title: [Concerning the T]welve Judges [of] the Father
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a systematic cosmological list of the Twelve Judges (a numbered emanational schema) with brief narrative functions for each—typical of the older correspondential-teaching layer. A late drift appears at the end: an explicit hortatory application to the audience (¶16), and an institutional intrusion (“holy church”) within the otherwise cosmic description of the Light Mind (¶13).

chapters.title: Concerning the Eighteen Great Thrones of all the Fathers
chapters.note: The chapter is largely a systematic, numbered cosmological list (18 thrones: 9 in the outer aeons, 9 in the zone) — this is strongly CORE in voice and structure. It is wrapped by a hagiographic/frame opening (¶1) and concluding doxological/summarizing material (¶11, ¶18), and it culminates in an explicitly institutional-hagiographic identification of the ninth throne in the zone with the present apostle in the holy church (¶17), consistent with the chapter-level editorial-fatigue drift.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Garments
chapters.note: Short chapter dominated by cosmological-mechanical teaching about the Living Spirit’s three ‘garments’ (wind, fire, water) and their deployment across the zone. Only the first paragraph contains a clear dialogue/frame attribution and direct address to disciples, which appears secondary to the underlying teaching narrative.

chapters.title: Concerning the Summons, in which Limb of the Soul it descended to the First Man.
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological teaching about the First Man as head of the living soul’s limbs, with internal correspondential analogies (head/limbs, air/breath, tower/Pillar of Glory) and a fivefold noetic set (mind, thought, insight, counsel, consideration). The only clear late layer is the opening dialogue-question frame with an appeal to “scriptures.” One paragraph (¶7) is more mythic-narrative in tone but still stays cosmos→cosmos (no institutional application), so it is retained as core with mild uncertainty noted.

chapters.title: Concerning the Seven Works of the Living Spirit
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a compact, systematic enumeration of the Living Spirit’s cosmic “seven works” (plus an additional end-time work), in an impersonal cosmological register. The main later material is the dialogue/frame attribution at the opening and a concluding beatitude-style blessing that reads like an editorial devotional tag rather than the older expository substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Things that he constructed with the hard Bodies of the Rulers
chapters.note: A very short, largely intact cosmological list-teaching: five cosmic constructions made by the Living Spirit from the hard bodies of the Rulers. The only clear late element is the formulaic dialogue/attribution opener in ¶1.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ten Things that the Ambassador began by his Advent
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely a compact, numbered cosmological sequence describing ten system-events initiated by the Third Ambassador’s advent (ships, wheels, separation of Night/Day, fall of Sin/abortions, transmigrations). Apart from a brief formulaic opener, there is no exhortation, institutional application, or NT overlay; several items are lacunose.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Works of the Ambassador
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a compact, systematic fourfold enumeration of cosmological effects of the Ambassador’s self-manifestation (image, firmament-doors, purification/releasing of Light, appearance of the Light Ship/Living Soul). The only clear later material is the hagiographic/dialogue-style attribution in ¶1, which frames an otherwise core teaching sentence.

chapters.title: Concerning the Wheel that exists in front of the King of Honour
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly systematic cosmological exposition: the Wheel before the King of Honour, its seals, and its function for binding/diagnosing the rulers and revealing the five shining men through the zone. The only clear later material is the dialogue-attribution frame (“Again the apostle speaks…”) at the start of ¶1, which is removed in extraction. No NT citation or institutional/pastoral application appears in the surviving text.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Zones.
chapters.note: The chapter is overwhelmingly a systematic cosmological teaching on the three-zone construction of the universe (Darkness powers → sons of the Man → sons of the Living Spirit), with only a brief hagiographic/dialogue-style incipit. No NT citations or pastoral/application pivots appear; the mappings remain cosmos→cosmos throughout. The final paragraph is fragmentary (lacunae) but still within the same structural exposition (King of Honour in the firmaments/universe).

chapters.title: Concerning the Light Mind and the Apostles and the Saints
chapters.note: The chapter’s oldest substrate dominates the middle: a systematic macrocosm↔microcosm correspondence (universe-as-human; five/six-fold sons; watch-district rebellions; then the body’s five-member binding and the Light Mind’s reversal). The opening Q&A and the closing apostolate-boast are hagiographic frame; the second-half drift (¶44–50) is clearly institutional/pastoral (church officers, rebuke, community management). Several paragraphs are MIXED where the editor appends institutional application (church/apostles persecution; idolatry polemic) to otherwise cosmological teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Days and the Two Deaths
chapters.note: Despite a formulaic dialogue opening, this chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological-esoteric periodization (three “days” / two “deaths”) expressed in impersonal, structural terms (First Man descent, purification cycle, new aeon, unveiling, separation in fire). The only clear late material is the dialogue frame (¶1–3) and a moralizing/NT-colored tail in the “second death” description (¶15).

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Things that were established by the Light
chapters.note: The chapter is overwhelmingly eschatological-cosmological teaching in an impersonal, systematic threefold structure (new earth/coffin/final lump and eternal separation). Aside from a brief hagiographic opening, there is no clear institutional or NT overlay; the “sinners/condemned by deeds” language reads as part of the cosmological mechanics rather than pastoral regulation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Blows that befell the Enemy because of the Light.
chapters.note: The chapter is essentially a compact, systematic eschatological teaching: a threefold sequence of defeats/bindings of the Enemy by the Light. Only the opening dialogue-attribution (“Once again he turned, and says:”) functions as late compilation frame; the rest stays cosmos→cosmos (wars, binding, dissolution in fire, final separation and confinement) without institutional/pastoral application.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Vessels
chapters.note: Dominantly core cosmological-mechanical exposition (Living Spirit’s three garments managing discharge/sweeping of the three dark vessels) expressed through extended correspondential analogies (doctor/medicines; child in womb/garments). Later compilation frame appears in the opening and in speech-attribution seams (¶1–2, ¶13), and a clear late application/pastoral drift appears in the second-half advantages list where the teaching is applied to contemporary human conditions ("today"), ascetic practice (fasting), and institutional roles (apostles).

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly the technical cosmological teaching layer: a stepwise account of how the Father of Life/Living Spirit discharges, gathers, and confines the three dark vessels, leaving measurable residues in the cosmos. The only later material is the dialogue apparatus (“disciples…”, “apostle…”, “enlightener…”) and brief audience-address cues; there is no NT citation and no institutional/pastoral extension.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sea Giant
chapters.note: Aside from a brief hagiographic opener, this chapter is a continuous cosmological-mechanical exposition: how the three wheels are turned and washed, how the waste is deposited in the sea, how the sea giant is formed and sealed with astral impressions, and the threefold function of the giant within the cosmic architecture. No NT citation formulas, no institutional application, and the analogical coin/craftsman comparison remains internal to the system (cosmos→cosmos). The high chapter-level ‘fatigue’ signal is not borne out by clear pastoral grafting here; the main late element is the opening frame.

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a single impersonal cosmological sequence: fore-prepared containment-places are constructed by the Powers of Light for specific Dark vessels/beings before they descend or arise, binding them until the end/dissolution of the universe. No NT citation, hagiographic dialogue frame, or church-institutional application appears. One brief didactic imperative at the start (¶1) reads like a later instructional bridge but does not alter the underlying substrate teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely a compact, impersonal sequence of pre-temporal appointments within the Manichaean cosmic plan (Ambassador, ships, Judge, astral fate, destroyers, Builder). The only clear late/polemical reach beyond the closed cosmic system is the clause about "the sects" (¶5), which applies the ordination of Christ to the editor’s contemporary religious landscape.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four great Things
chapters.note: Nearly the entire chapter is systematic cosmological exposition: a fourfold apportioning of the "ruling-power" across cosmic structures, followed by a mechanical rationale for suspending the leaders on the stellar wheel and an extended king/kingdom analogy to express proportional balance. Only the opening dialogue attribution is hagiographic frame; there is no NT citation or institutional/pastoral extension here (despite the chapter-level fatigue warning).

chapters.title: Concerning the Conduits.
chapters.note: The chapter is overwhelmingly a systematic cosmological-mechanical exposition of three ‘conduits/roots’ linking heavens, earths, trees, flesh, and the wheel of stars. Later material is mainly the dialogue/hagiographic apparatus (speaker attributions, disciples’ petitions). No NT citation overlay appears; the few frame formulas are detachable without disturbing the internal cosmos→cosmos mapping logic.

chapters.title: Concerning the Wheel and the Conduits
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly core mechanical teaching: a brief Q&A frame introduces a cosmological problem (wheel vs. conduits), followed by an impersonal explanation using analogies (ship/water; bird/air) to describe why pneumatic conduits are not cut or entangled. Only minimal dialogue attributions appear as later framing.

chapters.title: Concerning these Names: God, Rich One, and Angel; who they are.
chapters.note: The chapter is largely a systematic, internal-to-the-cosmic-system taxonomy of three naming-levels (god/rich one/angel) across successive emanational sequences. It is wrapped in a hagiographic Q&A opening (¶1–2) and contains two dialogue-attribution seams (¶3, ¶10) that must be stripped. The late/Christian-leaning vocabulary in ¶9 (“apostolate”) reads as Mani-community diction applied to a still-cosmological mission sequence rather than an NT citation or institutional graft.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a compact cosmological battle-teaching about the First Man’s five garments (living Fire plus four auxiliaries). The only clear later material is a brief hagiographic dialogue/frame opener. Despite the chapter-level fatigue signal, the surviving paragraphs after the opener remain cosmos→cosmos exposition; paragraph 5 is flagged by the pipeline for “application” but reads as internal cosmological continuation (air strengthening the four).

chapters.title: Concerning the [ ... ] of the Light
chapters.note: This chapter is largely an editorial moral/application unit (unity among hearers) built on a short cosmological premise: the Light’s inherent concord versus the Darkness’ self-division. The core substrate is preserved mainly as statements about internal harmony/order in the Light-realm and internal disunity in the Darkness-realm; the shift to analogy with "the kingdom of this world" and direct second-person exhortation marks later application.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly core cosmological teaching: First Man’s descent and the stripping of the storehouses, followed by correspondential analogies (marsh; human body/head and limbs; corpse). The only clear later material is the formulaic dialogue-attribution opening in ¶1, which functions as hagiographic frame around an otherwise core paragraph. Despite the chapter-level ‘fatigue’ signal, no explicit institutional/pastoral or NT overlay appears in the surviving paragraphs.

chapters.title: [Concerning] the Quality of the Garments
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly cosmological-architectonic teaching (mixture of Light/Darkness; ordering of garments/firmaments; artisan metaphors for the Living Spirit/Father of Life; final separation). The only clear later layer is a brief dialogue-attribution frame at the start of ¶1, which must be stripped. The extended carpenter/architect metaphors (¶3–¶4) remain within cosmos→cosmos exposition (no institutional/NT anchoring), though they are rhetorically elaborated and could be a secondary expansion within the teaching tradition.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fashioning of Adam
chapters.note: This chapter is predominantly cosmological teaching about why the Third Ambassador displayed his Image, how the rulers copied it to fashion Adam and Eve without the consent of Greatness, and how other composite life-forms arose without sexual intercourse. The only clear later layer is the disciples’ framed question (¶1) and a brief pedagogical closing (¶8). No NT citation formulas appear; the long “free woman” simile functions as an internal correspondential exposition rather than an institutional/pastoral application, though it may be a later rhetorical elaboration within the teaching tradition.

chapters.title: Concerning Saklas and his Powers
chapters.note: Chapter is largely dominated by systematic cosmological/anthropological teaching: (a) how Sin/Matter retained the seal of the Ambassador’s image through its descent and generative transmission, and (b) a long correspondential microcosm-teaching of the senses as ‘storehouses’ with guards at bodily gates, culminating in Light Mind/Living Spirit taking control from Sin. Strong late drift appears at the end: a clear exhortation paragraph, and an ecclesial-sounding ‘psalms/prayers/hymns/charity’ paragraph that applies the sensory doctrine to community practice. Several paragraphs are MIXED only because of dialogue-attribution formulas (‘the enlightener says/speaks’), which are stripped from the extracted core_text.

chapters.title: Concerning the Generation of Adam.
chapters.note: The oldest teaching substrate here is the astrological-cosmological mechanism explaining changing human stature/longevity via a fivefold hierarchy of zodiacal time-authorities (year/month/day/hour/moment) (¶2–6). Dialogue attributions are later frame (¶1, ¶8, ¶12) and are stripped where they introduce otherwise core material (¶3, ¶10). The second half shows clear editorial fatigue: a homiletic/end-times application and moralizing critique of contemporary humans (¶7, ¶11) plus renewed Q&A framing (¶8–9).

chapters.title: The Four Powers that grieve
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a formulaic dialogue frame, then preserves a substantial core cosmological teaching (Mother of Life; First Man) describing divine grief within the Light–Darkness conflict. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: it shifts to Mani’s self-presentation and the suffering of the institutional “holy church,” then to a Christianized eschatological warning (gehenna/repentance), suggesting later community expansion beyond the older substrate.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Elements that wept
chapters.note: The chapter’s dominant layer is a coherent, systematic fourfold cosmological teaching (the elements/garments of the First Man weeping at four fixed cosmic moments). It is wrapped in a brief dialogue-frame opening and ends with an editorial/pastoral turn that applies the teaching to the apostolic mission and a moral admonition—consistent with the strong chapter-level “editorial fatigue” drift in the second half.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Fathers; what they are like.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a systematic correspondential teaching (body-faculties mapped to cosmic beings/structures). The only clear late layer is the dialogue/lecture framing: the opening attribution to “the apostle…to his disciples” and the closing “Behold, I have shown to you…”. No Gospel citation formulae or institutional (church) applications appear; “Jesus the Splendour” functions as a cosmological being, not NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Garment of the Waters: how great is its Measure.
chapters.note: This chapter is a hagiographic-historical riverbank scene used to introduce a dense cosmological teaching about the elemental garment of Water. The core substrate concentrates in ¶6–10 (with a small fragment in ¶8): a systematic account of First Man’s deployment of elemental garments against the rulers, including the sevenfold river-measure and the binding of the giants. The opening/closing (¶1–3, ¶12) are clearly editorial frame; ¶11 is a later devotional/exhortative wrap rather than impersonal system-teaching. One intra-Manichaean citation (“Great Gospel”) in ¶6 is a later compilation marker embedded inside otherwise core cosmology.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Rocks
chapters.note: This chapter is predominantly a compact cosmological-cosmic stability teaching (three "rocks" fixed into the universe). The second-half pastoral drift is localized in ¶5, where the third rock is redefined as a support of the "holy church"—an institutional application that breaks the cosmos→cosmos mapping and reads like an editorial extension of the otherwise systematic triad.

chapters.title: Concerning Love.
chapters.note: Core teaching dominates the middle and end with a cosmological definition of Love (as the Father of Greatness) and Hate (as the first Death/Darkness-principle) operating in the time of mixture. The chapter opens with a standard dialogue/frame question. A major later graft applies the definition of love to the holy church and the apostle and then anchors it with an explicit written Gospel saying (NT overlay).

chapters.title: [Concerning Adam]
chapters.note: Apart from a brief formulaic dialogue opening (¶1), the chapter is a continuous, systematic teaching sequence: a threefold distinction in Adam followed by a sevenfold statement of the rulers’ intent in forming him. The diction stays cosmos→cosmos (image of the Ambassador, elements, zodiac/stars, rulers, ascent of light) without pivoting to institutional or contemporary-world application; thus nearly the entire chapter reads as teaching-core rather than later pastoral extension or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sun.
chapters.note: The chapter contains a substantial enumerative teaching core (seven benefits of the Sun; seven evils of the Night; five archetypes; three further archetypes corresponding to the mystery of the Father). It is wrapped in a hagiographic dialogue frame and repeatedly interrupted by editorial application/polemic against “the sects” and by a late Christian overlay at the end (a ‘saviour’ saying; ‘children of the day/light’). The second-half application drift matches the fatigue signal: the cosmological-cosmological correspondences remain, but are increasingly turned into exhortation and sectarian contrast.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador.
chapters.note: The chapter opens and closes with hagiographic dialogue frame, while the central teaching (¶2–¶6) gives a systematic correspondential exposition: daily solar rising/setting as the cosmic ‘first’ and ‘last’ moments (First Man’s descent/battle; Last Statue’s ascent/consummation). A clear late pastoral/application graft appears in ¶7 (direct address + imperative exhortation to preach/repent).

chapters.title: Concerning the Light-Giver.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic framing and pastoral/application material: a homiletic sun analogy is immediately used to identify the speaker (“I”) with the light-giver and to exhort love/charity toward the elect. There is no systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping (degree structures, world-lists, metal/taste/face correspondences, etc.), and the rhetoric repeatedly reaches into institutional identity (“elect”, “my children”, exhortation).

chapters.title: Concerning Fire.
chapters.note: A compact five-fold, impersonal classification of the operations of fire. Aside from the brief dialogue/frame attribution in ¶1, the chapter is a self-contained systematic teaching sequence with no NT citation, no institutional application, and no cosmos→contemporary-world pointing.

chapters.title: Concerning the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac and the Five Stars
chapters.note: The chapter is largely systematic cosmological teaching (zodiac and planets derived from the five worlds of Darkness; distribution by fours; effects on creatures). The main secondary layer is the Kephalaia dialogue/lecture frame (apostle/disciple setup and first-person recap formulas). No NT citation overlay appears; no explicit church-institution seam is present.

chapters.title: Concerning the Body: It was constructed after the Pattern of the Universe.
chapters.note: Core layer is dominant: systematic microcosm–macrocosm correspondences (body↔cosmic geography; five watch-stations; four bodily worlds with 7 rulers each; zodiacal body maps; demonic rulers causing illness). Clear later strata: (a) hagiographic dialogue frame (¶1, ¶30, ¶37); (b) an ethical/self-mastery application section explicitly keyed to the Elect and moral subduing (¶18–22), plus minor didactic asides inside otherwise core material (several MIXED cuts). No NT/Gospel overlay appears here.

chapters.title: Concerning the Gathering in of the [E]lements.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly the systematic eschatological mechanics of ascent: a chained sequence of gatherings from element to element and then through named salvific hypostases (Answer/Summons/Mind/Pillar/First Man/Ambassador) to the Aeons. Only the opening dialogue attribution is a later Kephalaia frame wrapper; the teaching itself stays cosmos→cosmos throughout with no institutional or NT overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the worn and torn apart Garments, or the tattered Clothes, or the Elements, the Cross, and the rest too.
chapters.note: The chapter has a clear hagiographic/Q&A frame (¶1–6) introducing a technical glossary, followed by a sustained core teaching block (¶7–15) defining successive names of the Light-soul/power by mapping each name to a specific cosmological function/state (Pillar of Glory, rulers/firmaments, three earths, Porter, three garments of wind/fire/water, bound Light in dry/moist, summons/obedience, vegetative life as ‘slain soul’, and final reunification). Despite the chapter-level ‘fatigue’ signal, the latter paragraphs remain cosmological/eschatological rather than institutional; the drop appears to be a vocabulary-list artifact rather than a genuine pastoral graft here.

chapters.title: Concerning the Envy of Matter
chapters.note: Core substrate is concentrated in ¶2–4 (and a definitional remnant in ¶1 and ¶8): Matter/Envy as a primordial Dark nature attacking key cosmic-historical figures (First Man; Image of the Ambassador; Adam). From ¶5 onward the chapter shifts into Christian/biographical/institutional application (Christ/cross; Mani and his church; catechumens; exhortation), matching the strong chapter-level editorial fatigue signal (pastoral drift in the second half).

chapters.title: Concerning the living Fire: It is present in Eight Places.
chapters.note: Dominantly CORE: a systematic enumerative teaching locating the living fire in eight cosmic stations (Light Land, Father, First Man/Perfect Man, the two light ships, Living Spirit’s descent gear, new earth foundations, and an eschatological manifestation). Only the opening dialogue attribution (“the apostle speaks”) is later FRAME wrapping; the rest stays cosmos→cosmos with no institutional or NT overlay.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Letter (?)]
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a standard dialogue frame, then preserves a compact core teaching on the primordial “summons” and “answer” exchanged between the Living Spirit and the First Man as foreknowing “letters” containing all events. The second half shows strong editorial fatigue: the letter motif is extended to the holy church, its good works, and direct exhortation about prayer—an institutional/pastoral graft that mimics the earlier teaching syntax but points outward to contemporary community practice.

chapters.title: [Conce]rning Lord Manichaios: how he journeyed.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly hagiographic/biographical travel narrative about Mani’s summons by Shapur and subsequent missionary journeys, with no systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential exposition. Two paragraphs embed a Johannine (Jn 3) light/darkness saying, which marks a Christian overlay. The chapter ends with direct audience exhortation/prayer and mention of the holy church (pastoral drift consistent with the chapter-level fatigue score).

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Four Kingdoms
chapters.note: This chapter is essentially a homiletic/pastoral exhortation built around a Gospel saying about giving bread and water, extended to Manichaean institutional categories (disciple/saints/catechumen) and reward-at-the-last-day logic. It contains no systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping or impersonal cosmological mechanics characteristic of the oldest teaching substrate; the second half shows strong pastoral drift (alms, fellowship, catechumens, blessing/exhortation).

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Things over which People kill each other.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later homiletic/application material (ethical description of worldly obsessions + exhortation to accept “faith” and the “physician”). It lacks the hallmark substrate feature of systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping (degree-structures, realm-to-realm correlations, etc.). The only clearly identifiable distinct layer is the hagiographic dialogue frame in ¶1; the remainder reads as moral/pastoral instruction rather than the oldest cosmological teaching substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fasting of the Saints
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by late institutional/pastoral instruction on fasting (including weekly practice and alms), wrapped in a standard dialogue opening. Two paragraphs preserve older doctrinal kernels in a more impersonal, process-oriented voice: the mechanics of purification of the soul/light in relation to food and the undefiled condition of the Children of Light. The numbered 'four works' structure appears to be an editorial pastoral organization into which these kernels were fitted.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Commandments of Righteousness
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly institutional/disciplinary (elect vs. catechumens; fasting, prayer, alms; prohibitions; donations to the church). Even where Manichaean cosmological terms appear (Cross of Light; sun and moon as light-givers), they function as practical piety and community regulation rather than impersonal cosmos→cosmos correspondential exposition. The strong editorial-fatigue drift and the seam-flagged final paragraph reinforce a late pastoral compilation with no recoverable pre-compilation substrate in these paragraphs.

chapters.title: The Chapter of Fasting, for it engenders a Host of Angels
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame plus institutional/pastoral material about fasting practice, ecclesial leadership responsibility, and avoiding sin in directing church works (building, alms). Even the seemingly “mechanistic” claim about fasting ‘engendering seven angels’ is anchored to church categories (elect, catechumens, lord’s day) and presented inside a first-person administrative narrative, not as impersonal cosmos→cosmos correspondential exposition. No recoverable pre-compilation substrate layer is visible in this excerpt.

chapters.title: The Chapter of Righteous [Judgement]
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by late dialogical frame and pastoral/institutional admonition about reprimand, anger, and repentance. Only one paragraph (¶9) presents a self-contained cosmological mechanism (the heavenly light-givers displaying two aspects to purify the soul/powers), which fits the older correspondential-cosmological substrate. A Matthean saying (Mt 6:21) appears in ¶10, marking Christian overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning the Man who is ugly in his Body, [but] beautiful [in his Soul].
chapters.note: Most of the chapter is hagiographic scene-setting (Mani in a public assembly) plus moral admonition culminating in an explicit Gospel saying (NT overlay). The oldest recoverable teaching layer here is concentrated in the impersonal, technical exposition of pearl formation (¶9–14, with a dialogue-attribution stripped in ¶9) and the cosmological return/rest of liberated souls (¶17). The later editor then applies the pearl imagery to the holy church and apostles (¶15–16) and ends with direct exhortation (¶18).

chapters.title: Concerning Wisdom; it is far superior when on the Tongue than in the Heart of the Person.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a non-institutional teaching unit (child-in-womb and fire-in-wood analogies) explaining why wisdom increases when expressed. The main late material is the Kephalaia dialogue apparatus (disciple petitions, apostle-attribution formulas, and the formulaic closing). No NT citation overlay and no ecclesial/pastoral graft is present; the core here is homiletic-correspondential rather than systematic cosmological mapping.

chapters.title: Concerning the Cross of Light: [...] trample upon it.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later pastoral/institutional application (missions, alms collection, elect/catechumen practice) wrapped in a dialogue frame, with marked pastoral drift in the second half. The oldest recoverable teaching here is mainly a cosmological-soteriological kernel: the Living Soul/Cross of Light can undergo necessary distress for healing/liberation without reckoning it as sin (medical analogy), plus a (partly lacunose) mechanism linking destructive speech to demonic binding. One explicit Gospel citation is a later Christian overlay.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Man who asks: Why [am] I sometimes at peace, and troubled at other times?
chapters.note: The chapter is built as a framed Q&A. The opening and closing are hagiographic frame; the disciple’s long self-description includes institutional piety (fasting, psalms, prayers) and reads as later pastoral coloration. The oldest teaching substrate is concentrated in the explanatory mechanism: purification by the Light Mind, disturbances via birth-signs/stars and the ‘roots/conduits’ of the heavenly powers, and the mixed composition of food and drink affecting inner states—plus the notable doctrine of ‘justified souls’ present in nourishment (transmigration/merit language).

chapters.title: Concerning the Alms, that [ ... ] life in the Church.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional/pastoral exposition about alms, the holy church, and catechumens (¶¶2–6, 11), wrapped in a hagiographic opening (¶1). The oldest teaching substrate appears as a self-contained cosmological mechanism of ascent and rest: the Living Soul in mixture can exit only through the Sun and Moon, and these light-givers rest finally in the Land of Light (¶¶7–10).

chapters.title: Concerning the Catechumen who found fault with the Elect: why he is angry.
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a situational pastoral/homiletic piece (catechumen vs. Elect), wrapped in narrative frame. The only recoverable older substrate is a small cluster of dualist-anthropological statements (divinity from the heights; alien body; the “two essences”) embedded inside exhortation and institutional categories (Elect/saints). No systematic cosmos→cosmos mapping sequence appears here; the correspondential tree image functions as moral application, not cosmological exposition.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a late debate-frame (Nazorean interlocutor + ‘apostle’ dialogue) and ethical-judicial argumentation rather than systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential exposition. The only explicit scriptural overlay is the Gospel saying about treasure/heart (Mt 6:21), and adjacent eschatological vocabulary (“gehenna”, “life eternal”) likely belongs to the same Christian-lexical stratum. No recoverable oldest correspondential substrate is present.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fifteen Paths; and whether the Catechumen would have avoided causing his Wealth to go on the Three Paths to Gehenna
chapters.note: Only a small core substrate survives here: a compact, systematic cosmological teaching on the fifteen paths in the “zone” and the three waste-paths to the gehennas (¶2–4, embedded inside a question-summary). The remainder is dominated by later institutional soteriology about elect/catechumens, the apostle’s pre-selection of “the entire church,” seals of faith, transmigration as purification, and practical piety (fasting/prayer/alms), matching the chapter’s strong pastoral drift and Gardner’s redaction/buddhist-connection flags.

chapters.title: Also concerning the Catechumen; shall he be saved in a single Body?
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly institutional/pastoral (catechumen discipline, fasting, alms, church protection, merit accounting) wrapped in dialogue frame. The only recoverable older substrate consists of brief, more impersonal eschatological mechanism statements about post-mortem ascent and purification (firmaments/heavens; purification; ‘light image’; land of rest). There is explicit Christian overlay via a Pauline citation (¶4) and a likely Matthean proverb echo embedded in an otherwise mechanistic sequence (¶20).

chapters.title: The Apostle is asked: Why when you drew every thing in the Picture (- Book), did you not draw the Purification of the Catechumens who shall be cleansed by Transmigration?
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional categories (catechumen/elect) and a hagiographic dialogue frame. The eschatological imagery (Judge, dispenser of justice, gehenna) is expressed in Christian-derived terms, and the explanation of transmigration is presented as catechumen instruction rather than impersonal cosmological system-mapping. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate is present at paragraph granularity.

chapters.title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give an Offering to the Saints, shall I inflict a Wound on the Alms?
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by the Q&A frame plus institutional/pastoral concerns (catechumen → elect alms-offering; anxiety about “sinning” against the Living Soul; absolution language; church vocabulary). The extended judge/enemy/doctor analogy functions as moral-pastoral justification for alms preparation rather than a cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping or a systematic cosmological exposition. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate can be cleanly extracted here.

chapters.title: Concerning the Purification of these Four Elements [that have been place]d in the Flesh.
chapters.note: This kephalaion is dominated by an impersonal, systematic correspondential teaching layer: the four elements’ pollution-discharge chain (element → bodily secretion → affect → bodily condition) and the mechanism of purification in the body/new man. It is wrapped by a brief hagiographic sitting-scene frame (¶1) and closed by an institutional application contrasting elect vs. sinners (¶9).

chapters.title: The Apostle asks his Disciples: What is Cloud?
chapters.note: Dominantly CORE: a systematic fivefold cosmological-correspondential mapping of clouds to the five light elements (fire, water, wind, light, mingled air), including the mechanics of purification of Lives, the stripping/descent of rulers, angelic seizure, and confinement in the seven outer ditches/paths. FRAME appears in the formulaic opening, the disciples’ question, and the closing doxology; a few teaching paragraphs are wrapped with dialogue/imperative meta-speech (treated as MIXED). No NT/Christian citation overlay; no institutional/pastoral grafting.

chapters.title: The Three Earths that Exist, they bear Fruit.
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is concentrated in ¶¶2–3 (and the teaching portion of ¶1): a threefold correspondential schema of “earth/field” (physical earth → Living Soul in the cosmic zone → later grafted ‘holy church’). ¶4 is a classic editorial seam: it mimics the same “earth/field + farmer” pattern but crosses from cosmos→institution (holy church, elect, catechumens), so the whole paragraph is late pastoral extension despite its cosmological diction (Light Mind). ¶5 is explicit exhortation/application to the audience (preach, toil), hence pastoral.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Creations of the Flesh: the ones that were brought forth [...]; and the ones that were begotten by the Abortions; and the ones that were formed of themselves.
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely a systematic, impersonal teaching sequence classifying animal/plant generation and nourishment within a Manichaean cosmological mechanism (Ambassador, rulers/powers, “thought” descending). Only the brief dialogue-introduction is later hagiographic frame.

chapters.title: What is Virginal; or, otherwise, what is Continent?
chapters.note: The chapter is built as a five-step definitional ladder (“virginal” vs “continent”) mostly in a systematic cosmological/soteriological register. The opening Q&A is hagiographic frame. The final two steps drift into community-institutional categories (“elect”) and then human sexual practice; these are later applications layered onto the underlying degree-structure teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning Transmigration
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic/dialogue frame and institutional-pastoral instruction aimed at catechumens vs. sinners. Even where Light/fire imagery appears (¶5), it is embedded in a catechetical comparison of ecclesial categories (catechumens/sinners) rather than an impersonal cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping or systematic cosmological mechanism. No recoverable oldest correspondential substrate can be cleanly extracted from these paragraphs as presented.

chapters.title: Concerning the Dragon with Fourteen Heads; what it is and [...]
chapters.note: The chapter’s teaching substrate is a systematic microcosm mapping: the “dragon” is a spiritual force/thought associated with the body, having fourteen “heads” (sense/torso faculties) and five “dens” (internal organs). This is largely CORE in ¶3–¶6, with Q&A framing in ¶1–¶2 and a closing disciple-response in ¶9. ¶7–¶8 show late drift toward exhortation and Manichaean institutional labels (“elect”), consistent with the strong chapter-level editorial fatigue signal.

chapters.title: [Concer]ning why, if the Person shall look down into Water, [ ... ]
chapters.note: Dominantly correspondential-cosmological teaching: a natural phenomenon (reflection/shadow) is mapped onto cosmic process (the Summons descending to the Worlds of Darkness; the Obedience ascending to the Living Spirit; astral/zodiacal generation; embodiment from earth/abyss). Later compilation frame survives mainly as dialogue attributions and didactic address (“I reveal… to you”), which can be cleanly stripped. No clear NT overlay appears in the extant paragraphs; the main secondary layer here is the hagiographic dialogue frame and occasional application voice.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light Mind, why it does not exercise Foreknowledge for the Saint as for the Apostle?
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later dialogical framing and community-directed, practical/ethical reasoning about why the Light Mind does not grant foreknowledge to the elect. It repeatedly maps cosmological language (Light Mind) onto ecclesial roles (apostle/elect/holy church) and contemporary risks (dissension, profit, magicians/fortune-tellers), rather than giving an impersonal, systematic cosmos→cosmos exposition. No recoverable correspondential substrate appears.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Wonders that the Light Mind shall display in the Elect
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by institutional/ethical material (preaching, brethren, church discipline, legal excommunication) expressed as a fivefold list of virtues/signs in the Elect. Only one short paragraph (¶7) reads like an older cosmological-soteriological mechanism statement (Light Mind acting as an agent purifying/choosing the new man) without overt church/institutional anchoring. The opening uses a standard apostolic attribution frame.

chapters.title: Concerning Food: It shall be allocated to Five Products of the human Body.
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic opening, the chapter is a compact, systematic fivefold teaching: food entering the body is apportioned into five 'productions'. The voice is impersonal and expository, with numbered structure and no NT citation, institutional application, or exhortation—consistent with the older teaching substrate (cosmos/body mechanism rather than church practice).

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Things that are great with Mankind, as they are running all the time, in that they [ ... ]
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by later Christian-connected comparison (Christ-name practices) and hagiographic self-presentation of Mani (“I, Manichaios…”, apostolate, rhetorical boasting, promise to believers). No systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping or impersonal cosmological mechanism appears; the chapter reads as editorial-apologetic material rather than the oldest teaching substrate.

chapters.title: There is no Joy that shall remain in the World till the End.
chapters.note: Aside from a brief formulaic opening attribution, this chapter is a continuous, systematic cosmological exposition: during the time of mixture even the Sun and Moon cannot rejoice fully, because they behold (1) the Enemy’s rule in the cosmos and (2) the Living Soul’s ongoing oppression until final cleansing and fettering of Death.

chapters.title: Concerning the Form of the Word, that [ ... 30 ... ]
chapters.note: The chapter is essentially a compact correspondential/mechanistic teaching on how a spoken word is produced through five bodily members, reinforced by an analogy to five craftsmen producing a coin. Only the initial discourse-attribution formula in ¶1 belongs to the later hagiographic frame; the rest is impersonal, structural exposition without institutional application or NT citation.

chapters.title: Concerning the Seed Grain that shall be formed by the Elements, and also be destroyed by them
chapters.note: After a brief hagiographic dialogue header, the chapter is largely a compact cosmological teaching using the seed-grain/tree as a correspondential image for elemental formation and blight in the mixture. One paragraph (¶3) pivots from cosmic description to ecclesial actors (“teachers and the elect”), indicating a later institutional application grafted onto an older correspondential line.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fifty Lord's Days; to what Mysteries do they correspond? Or the Second (Fifty); to whose Sign (are they)?
chapters.note: The chapter opens with a formal Q&A frame about institutional fasting (catechumens/elect). The oldest layer appears chiefly in ¶2–¶4 as a numerical-cosmological exposition (five garments × five powers → twenty-five limbs/sons; ascent of the Summons/Answer/Obedience; living food). The second half (¶5–¶8) drifts strongly into institutional legitimation and then explicitly NT/apostolic exempla (apostles, Christ’s temptation, Simon the leper, tomb), matching the chapter’s high editorial-fatigue signal.

chapters.title: Concerning the Nourishment of the Person, for there are Powers in it [ ... / ... ]
chapters.note: This short chapter is dominated by systematic cosmological-physiological teaching (body as a purification apparatus; enumerated inner powers; cleansing/expulsion; transmigration mechanics). The only clear later material is a brief dialogue/frame attribution at the start of ¶1, which can be cleanly removed without damaging the teaching sequence.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Archetypes that occur in the Eye, and the Fifth that is hidden in them; to whom do they belong?
chapters.note: Highly fragmentary chapter. What survives is mainly a cosmological-correspondential teaching about perception (eye/pupil), fourfold structure plus a hidden fifth, and elemental/ontological assignments (Fire, Abyss/Darkness, Living Air/Light). The only clear later layer is the recurring dialogue-attribution formula (“Once again he speaks:”) plus brief audience-address/explanation rhetoric in ¶3; there is no institutional/pastoral extension and no NT overlay.

chapters.title: The Human is less than all the Things of the Universe, and he is rebellious beyond them all.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic travel narrative and polemical/theodicy application (humanity’s blasphemy; denying that demons come from God). The oldest cosmological substrate appears only in brief embedded fragments: (a) Jesus’ non-anthropocentric, cosmic ‘task’ in the great universe and his revelation to Adam and Eve; (b) compressed cosmology items (aeons/Greatness, Light vs Darkness, descent to the province of death) preserved inside later catechetical list-format; and (c) a short cosmological description of the Cross of Light embedded in a moral injunction. No paragraph is “pure core” without later framing; the core survives mostly as extractable fragments inside later catechesis.

chapters.title: The Chapter on whether any [Lig]ht comes from the Three Vessels.
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely a compact cosmological-mechanistic exposition (light-rays entering via gates/doors, firmament-by-firmament clarification, division into an taken-up portion vs cast-down portion). The only clearly later material is the dialogue frame and question prompt in ¶1, plus the brief dialogue attribution introducing the teaching in ¶2.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Images that are in the righteous Person.
chapters.note: Nearly the entire chapter is systematic anthropological-cosmological process teaching: a threefold structure (spiritual/psychic/corporeal) and the mechanics of purification of the living soul through these degrees, culminating in the action of the Light Virgin/Virgin of Light. Only the brief hagiographic speech-introduction is later frame.

chapters.title: The Catechumen asks the Apostle: will Rest come about for Someone who has come out of the Body, if the Saints pray over and make an Alms-offering for him?
chapters.note: The chapter is framed as a catechumen’s question about alms/prayer for the dead; the second half shows strong institutional/pastoral drift (editorial fatigue). The oldest recoverable substrate is preserved mainly in two archetypal “first/second entreaty” cosmological episodes (Mother of Life→Living Spirit; gods→Third Ambassador), plus a fragmented “third entreaty” sequence including Jesus the Splendour as a cosmic being. Later hands repeatedly pivot from cosmos→cosmos narration to cosmos→church practice (elect/catechumens, alms, remembrance, holy church), often as summary/charge paragraphs; a seam-flagged institutional extension appears at ¶42.

chapters.title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall not be sick; but if a Limb is cut he shall immediately be pained.
chapters.note: This chapter is largely dialogue frame (disciple question + apostolic response formulae + closing). The only recoverable older teaching-like content is a short correspondential analogy (body↔earth; limbs↔trees; regrowth varieties) explaining why some cuttings cause pain and others do not. It stays within natural/microcosmic correspondences and does not pivot to church institutions or Gospel citation, but it lacks the distinctive systematic cosmological architecture found in the strongest CORE strata; hence it is treated as a core fragment embedded in a later instructional frame.

chapters.title: Concerning why Some shall delay to come forth from the Body, and Others die in an instant.
chapters.note: Extremely fragmentary kephalaion dominated by dialogue frame/questions. Only ¶2 preserves a non-framing, enumerative explanation ("The second...") that likely belonged to the older systematic teaching about differentiated death/departure timings, but the cosmological mechanism is lost in lacunae; classification remains tentative.

Chapter 118 is almost entirely lost (only a few readable words in two fragments). No stable frame formulas, institutional/pastoral material, or NT-citation markers survive in the extant text; what remains looks like broken teaching prose (light/universe, possible numerical structuring: “seven…”, “these other three”). Any layering judgment is therefore highly uncertain and based mainly on absence of late markers rather than positive core structure.

chapters.title: Chapter 119: [ ... ]
chapters.note: The chapter preserves several mythic/cosmological statements about the First Man (approval in the Aeons of Light; sinlessness; steadfastness amid the worlds of Darkness; purification/separation work). But the core is repeatedly repurposed into an exemplar for the community (address to “my brothers and my limbs,” catechumen language, standing firm in the body), and the chapter ends with a clear hagiographic closing. Editorial fatigue is visible: the mid–late paragraphs shift from cosmological description to exhortation and institutional identity-markers.

chapters.title: Concerning the Two Essences
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by late polemical/application rhetoric against monotheism and by Christian/Gospel proof-texting (two-trees / five-trees, beloved son, holy spirit, last-day advent). The only recoverable substrate fragment is the bare cosmological axiom of the two primordial Essences (Light and Darkness), embedded inside a hagiographic vision-frame in ¶1. Strong editorial fatigue is visible: the second half concentrates exhortation and judgement language.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sect of the Basket
chapters.note: The chapter opens with hagiographic/narrative framing about a Babylonian presbyter and an explanation of the sect-name, then shifts into an applied analogy (universe-as-tree) used polemically about alms/identity (pastoral/application). The oldest teaching substrate appears mainly in the broken cosmological catalogue of angels/pillars/sea/earth and the twelve powers/three pillars material; however, paragraph 5 shows editorial wrapping (dialogue bridge) and a probable institutional intrusion (“holy church”), consistent with the strong chapter-level editorial-fatigue signal.

chapters.title: Concerning the 'Assent' and the 'Amen'
chapters.note: The chapter is dominated by late liturgical/pastoral exposition about congregational prayer, sealing, healing, and temptation; this matches the strong editorial-fatigue signal and Gardner’s “christian_connection” flag. A small core substrate survives where ‘assent’ and ‘amen’ are grounded in the cosmic archetypes Summons and Obedience as “portals” opening mercy for the First Man (and related Light beings). Paragraph 4 shows a clear pivot where the cosmic mechanism is extended into institutional ‘holy church/teacher’ identifications (a cosmos→contemporary-world crossing).
